intro: Dictation for nurses on a Mac means speaking and getting clean text at your cursor. Hold fn in Lazur, talk, and let go. The words land in whichever app you have open. Your employer decides which tools may touch patient information, so check that first. This guide covers where your shift time goes, where dictation helps, and the mistakes to avoid.
tldr: Hold fn, speak, and release. Clean text appears at your cursor in the app you are using.
Flowsheet work averaged 31.11% of a 12-hour shift in a 2025 study of EHR vendor logs.
Focus-group nurses put EHR documentation at 10% to 50% of their shift.
Ask your employer which tools can touch patient information before you dictate patient details.

blocks.text: How much of a nurse's shift goes to EHR documentation

A 2025 study in JMIR Nursing looked at four teaching hospitals in the northeastern US. It combined EHR vendor logs with focus groups. The vendor logs covered all inpatient nurses in the system, using data from February 2023. In those logs, time spent in flowsheets averaged 31.11% of a 12-hour shift. That is about 3 hours and 44 minutes of one shift spent in one part of the chart.

Flowsheets are the grids you fill in at set times. Blood pressure, intake, output, pain scores and turns all go there. Each entry is small. Together, they fill a shift. That is why the number is so high, even though no single entry feels like much.

The focus group gave a wider range. Twenty registered nurses took part, and 17 completed the demographic survey. They said 10% to 50% of their shift goes to documenting in the EHR, and many of them considered that appropriate. On a 12-hour shift, 10% is 1.2 hours and 50% is 6 hours. That spread matters. Your unit, your patient load and your EHR build all move where you land.
Where dictation helps and where it does not

Dictation does not fix a flowsheet grid. You still pick the right field and enter the right value. Where dictation helps is the narrative part of the work. That covers the shift summary, the update to your charge nurse, and the note you need before the next task pulls you away.

Test the idea on your own hands before you change your habits. The [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) gives you a number to compare. Keep the result. It helps when you decide which notes to speak and which to type.
How to dictate on a Mac with Lazur

Start with the basics. Hold fn, speak at a normal pace, and let go. Lazur turns your speech into text and places it at the cursor. It formats as it goes, so you can speak in full sentences and skip most of the punctuation.

items: Click into the field where the text should go. Lazur needs a cursor to type into.
Hold fn, wait a moment for the cursor to be ready, then speak.
Release fn when you finish the thought. Short holds are easier to check.
Read the text before you move on. Names, times, units and doses are the words that cost the most when they go wrong.

blocks.text: Hold long notes in parts. A few short holds are easier to proofread than one long hold. Keep the cursor in the right place between holds, or the second part lands in the wrong field.
Personal dictionary and snippets for nursing terms

Add the words your unit uses to your personal dictionary. Drug names, unit abbreviations, equipment names and your own surname are good candidates. Snippets handle phrases you repeat, such as your standard shift-end line. Clipboard slots hold text you paste more than once.
A dictionary should hold terms, never patient details. Store a drug name, not a patient's name.
When dictation gets a word wrong

It will get some words wrong. Medical terms, drug names and accents are the usual trouble spots. Do not fight it in the moment. Fix the word by hand, then add the correct form to your personal dictionary. Each fix you make now saves a correction later.
Speak the hard word slowly once, then carry on. Stopping to repeat a whole sentence often costs more time than a quick fix after. Use a read-back at the end to catch what the dictation missed.
A worked example: one message, hands full

Say you need to tell your charge nurse that the supply closet on the step-down unit is out of syringes. You are walking, your hands are full, and a spare moment is all you have. You hold fn and say it in one breath: the supply closet is out of syringes, and the pharmacy runner is late.

You release fn. The text lands in the message box with capital letters and full stops. You read it, then send it yourself. The whole job takes a single hold and a quick read. That is the point. You keep your attention on the floor.
Speaking loosely gives you loose text, even with clean formatting. Speak in short, complete thoughts, the way you would write them. Then read it back before you send.
Which apps and screens you will meet

Most nurses reach the chart in one of two ways. Some hospitals install a native Mac app. Epic Hyperspace is on the Mac App Store, and its listing requires macOS 14.0 or later. The listing shows version 100.2610.4, and it does not say whether your hospital uses it.

Search results suggest some hospitals reach the chart through a remote desktop client, such as Citrix or Omnissa Horizon. I could not confirm which hospitals do. If yours does, the screen you see comes from a server somewhere else. Dictation may still type at the cursor in that window. Test it with a sentence that has no patient details before you rely on it.

Email is the other screen many nurses open. Microsoft says over 95% of Microsoft 365 users have moved to the new Outlook for Mac. Its support page also says the legacy client stops working against Exchange Online starting October 2026. That date has already passed, so open Outlook and check which client you use. For the screen itself, see [Outlook on Mac](/apps/outlook).
Patient information comes first

Your employer sets the rules for patient data. This page does not, and neither does Lazur. Before you dictate anything with a patient name, room, date of birth or other identifier, ask your privacy or IT team whether the tool is approved for that use. An app that works well on your Mac is not automatically an app your hospital allows.

Know where audio goes. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers so it can answer you. Those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Your hospital may still say no. If it does, follow that answer, even if it differs from what this page says.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. That limits what it sees. It does not make a tool approved for patient information. If your policy says no, keep patient details out of Lazur and use the system your hospital names.
Mistakes nurses make with dictation

items: Dictating in a loud hallway. Background noise turns clean text into guesses. Step somewhere quieter, or wait until the alarm stops.
Trusting the first draft. Check names, times, units and doses every time, even when the text looks right.
Holding fn for one long note. Long holds hide mistakes. Break the note into parts you can read at a glance.
Charting in the wrong place. Dictated text is not the record. Put the note in the system your hospital requires.
Leaving a shared Mac unlocked. Lock the screen when you step away from a shared workstation.
Treating Lazur as a pair of hands. It points, guides and types text. It does not press buttons or operate other apps. You do that.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from speed. Slow down for the last few seconds of every note. That pause is where the errors get caught.
A routine for your next shift

A realistic shift has more asks than dictation. You will walk, point at buttons, check a policy and set a reminder. Pick the one that saves time at the moment you feel stuck. You do not need to use every feature on every shift.

items: Install Lazur from the [download page](/download). Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app.
Ask your IT or privacy team which tools you may use with patient information. Get the answer in writing.
Add your unit's terms to the personal dictionary. Leave out patient details.
Test one hold on a sentence with no patient details. Read it back before you trust it.
Compare [Pro and Power on the pricing page](/pricing) if you need more AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both.

blocks.text: Once the routine works, the chart still needs your judgment. Dictation only changes how the words reach the screen.

faq.question: Can I use dictation for nurses on a Mac inside Epic?
faq.answer: That depends on how your hospital gives you access to the chart. Lazur dictates at the cursor in any app that takes text. Whether dictation is allowed inside your EHR is a decision for your IT and privacy teams, so ask them before you try it with patient information.

faq.question: Is Lazur approved for patient information?
faq.answer: This page cannot answer that, and a Mac app listing cannot either. Your employer decides which tools may handle patient data. Ask your privacy or IT team in writing if you are unsure. Until they answer, keep patient details out of it.

faq.question: What happens to my audio when I dictate?
faq.answer: Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers so it can answer you. Those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Your hospital may still have rules about where that data goes, so check them.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons in the EHR for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It can draw a circle around a button and tell you what it does. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

faq.question: Which keys do I hold?
faq.answer: Hold fn to dictate. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows or Intel Macs?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned but not available yet.

faq.question: Does dictation cost extra?
faq.answer: Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans. AI actions are counted separately. See [pricing](/pricing) for the current plan details.

faq.question: Can I dictate a note without naming the patient?
faq.answer: You can, and it is a good habit. Your policy decides what counts as an identifier. Use only the details your employer allows, and keep names out of anything that is not an approved record.

faq.question: Where should I start if I am new to dictation?
faq.answer: Start with a message to a colleague that has no patient details. Read the text back, then try a short note in the approved system. Build up from there.

painPoints.title: Narrative notes get written in the gaps
painPoints.text: Updates and summaries happen while you walk. By the time you sit down, the detail has gone. Dictation catches the thought while it is still fresh.

day.result: Lazur works in its own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report. Check it against the written policy.

day.result: Text lands at the cursor with no names in it. Keep identifiers out of anything you dictate unless your policy says yes.

day.result: Lazur creates a Calendar event for Thursday at 16:30. Check the title and time before you close it.
